blocks.text: A bicycle designer pins a log-log chart on the wall, slides a ruler across it, and discards steel, aluminium and titanium in a few seconds because the carbon-fibre composite sits far above the line. Material property charts compress thousands of materials into one picture that can be read by eye.

blocks.markdown: An **Ashby-style chart** plots one material property against another, typically on logarithmic axes, with each material class shown as a region or bubble that spans the range of values found in that class. The most common is Young's modulus $E$ against density $\rho$. The log scales are essential because properties span many orders of magnitude (the modulus alone from 0.001 GPa for soft elastomers to above 1000 GPa for diamond).

blocks.caption: Typical values read from E-density charts; they are approximate and vary within each class.

blocks.markdown: **Where the classes lie.** Metals form a compact band, with moduli of about 10 to 400 GPa and densities of 2 to 20 Mg/m$^3$. Technical ceramics sit at similar densities but reach higher moduli. Polymers and elastomers lie low on the chart (about 0.001 to 10 GPa) at densities near 1 Mg/m$^3$. Composites bridge the gap: carbon-fibre laminates have low densities and moduli approaching those of metals. Foams and woods stretch down to lower densities. The position follows from bonding: strong ionic, covalent and metallic bonds give high moduli, while polymers deform by stretching weak secondary bonds.

blocks.title: Guideline for a performance index
blocks.text: A straight line drawn on the log-log chart along which a performance index $M$ has a constant value. For $M=E/\rho$ the line is $\log E=\log\rho+\log M$, with slope 1; for $M=E^{1/2}/\rho$ the slope is 2; for $M=E^{1/3}/\rho$ the slope is 3. Materials above and to the left of a line have a larger index.

blocks.caption: $C$: the value of the index on that line.

blocks.title: Reading a guideline through steel
blocks.prompt: A guideline of constant $E/\rho$ passes through steel ($E=210$ GPa, $\rho=7.85$ Mg/m$^3$). Where does carbon-fibre composite ($E=140$ GPa, $\rho=1.55$ Mg/m$^3$) lie relative to it?

steps.text: Find the index on the line.
At the composite's density the line gives the modulus $E_{line}=C\rho$.
Compare with the composite's actual modulus.

blocks.answer: The composite lies above the line: its modulus is 3.4 times the line value at that density, so it has 3.4 times the specific stiffness of steel.

blocks.title: Which candidates lie above a chosen guideline?
blocks.prompt: Select the materials in the table above with $E/\rho\ge40$ GPa per Mg/m$^3$.

steps.text: Compute $E/\rho$ for each: steel 26.8, Al 25.9, Ti 24.4, Mg 25.9, alumina 97, carbon composite 90, glass composite 21, nylon 2.2, HDPE 1.1.

blocks.answer: Only alumina and the carbon/epoxy composite lie above the line; note that the three common metals cluster together just below 27.

blocks.markdown: **Range within a class.** The extent of a bubble shows how much a property can be changed within a class by composition and processing. All steels have almost the same modulus (about 200 to 215 GPa) because modulus is set by bond stiffness and atomic packing, so a bubble for steels is tight. The same steels have yield strengths covering a factor of ten or more, because strength depends on microstructure, so a strength chart would show a tall bubble. In polymers, cross-linking, crystallinity and the glass transition produce a modulus range of three to four decades, so their bubble is large. Bubbles stretched along a slope-1 direction, as for foams and woods, show that porosity changes both modulus and density together.

items: Read charts on log axes: equal distances are equal ratios, not equal differences.
Slide a guideline of the correct slope to screen candidates: materials above it beat those below it.
The size and shape of a bubble show how much a property varies within the class, and what controls it.
A chart screens on one or two properties; strength, toughness, cost and process still need checking.

blocks.title: Chart values are typical
blocks.text: Bubbles show ranges, and values read from a chart are approximate. Use specific data for design calculations and treat the chart as a screening tool.

points: An $E$-$\rho$ chart puts metals and ceramics high, polymers and elastomers low, and composites between them, because bond stiffness sets modulus.
Guidelines of constant $E/\rho$ have slope 1 on log-log axes; materials above and to the left have higher specific stiffness, and a few metals cluster together near 26.
The shape and size of a class bubble show how much structure and processing can change a property within the class.

questions.stem: On a log-log chart of Young's modulus (vertical) against density (horizontal), where do the main material classes lie?

options.text: Metals and ceramics occupy the upper part of the chart, with polymers, elastomers and foams in the lower part, and composites bridging the gap at low density
Polymers have the highest moduli and the highest densities
All classes overlap in a single compact cluster
Ceramics have the lowest densities and moduli

questions.correctOptionText: Metals and ceramics occupy the upper part of the chart, with polymers, elastomers and foams in the lower part, and composites bridging the gap at low density

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the high stiffness of metallic, ionic and covalent bonds puts metals and ceramics high; secondary bonding in polymers puts them low.
distractorRationale.b: Polymers have low moduli (about 0.001 to 10 GPa) and low densities.
distractorRationale.c: The classes occupy distinct, partly overlapping regions spanning several decades of modulus.
distractorRationale.d: Technical ceramics are among the stiffest materials, with moduli of hundreds of GPa.

questions.explanation: The modulus reflects bond stiffness: strong primary bonds in metals and ceramics give 10 to 1000 GPa, while polymers rely on weak secondary bonds between chains and so lie at about 0.001 to 10 GPa. Composites such as carbon-fibre laminates combine low density with high stiffness, filling the region between polymers and metals.

questions.stem: A guideline for constant $E/\rho$ is drawn on a log-log chart of $E$ against $\rho$. What is its slope?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: $\log E=\log\rho+\log C$, a straight line of slope 1.
distractorRationale.b: This is the slope of the $E^{1/2}/\rho$ guideline.
distractorRationale.c: This does not arise from $E/\rho=C$; it would correspond to $E=C\rho^{1/2}$.
distractorRationale.d: A slope of zero would mean $E$ is constant regardless of density.

questions.explanation: Taking logarithms of $E/\rho=C$ gives $\log E=\log\rho+\log C$, so the line has slope 1 on log-log axes. Moving the line up or left (higher $E$ or lower $\rho$) improves the index, and every material on a given line has the same index.

questions.stem: Using $E/\rho$ (in GPa per Mg/m$^3$), which of these four has the largest specific stiffness? Values (E in GPa, density in Mg/m$^3$): steel (210, 7.85); tungsten (400, 19.3); a lead alloy (16, 11.3); a hardwood along the grain (12, 0.70).

distractorRationale.a: Correct: steel $210/7.85=26.8$ compared with 20.7, 1.4 and 17.1 for the others.
distractorRationale.b: Tungsten has the largest modulus but also a very high density, so its index is lower than steel's.
distractorRationale.c: Wood is light but not stiff enough to beat steel per unit mass: $12/0.70=17.1$.
distractorRationale.d: Lead is both dense and compliant, giving the lowest index.

questions.explanation: Specific stiffness is $E/\rho$: steel 26.8, tungsten 20.7, hardwood 17.1 and lead alloy 1.4 GPa per Mg/m$^3$. Highest modulus alone does not rank materials per unit mass; the density must be considered, so steel comes out ahead.

questions.stem: A guideline of constant $E/\rho$ is drawn through steel ($E=210$ GPa, $\rho=7.85$ Mg/m$^3$) on an $E$-$\rho$ chart. Calculate the modulus, in GPa, that lies on this line at a density of 1.74 Mg/m$^3$, the density of a magnesium alloy.
questions.explanation: Along the line $E/\rho=210/7.85=26.75$ GPa per Mg/m$^3$, so at $\rho=1.74$ the modulus is $26.75\times1.74=46.5$ GPa. A magnesium alloy with a modulus of 45 GPa lies just below this line, so it is marginally worse than steel for specific stiffness.

questions.stem: A hardwood has $E=12$ GPa along the grain and a density of 0.70 Mg/m$^3$ (typical values). Calculate its specific stiffness $E/\rho$ in GPa per Mg/m$^3$.
questions.explanation: The specific stiffness is $E/\rho=12/0.70=17.1$ GPa per Mg/m$^3$. This places it on a guideline below those of steel (26.8) and aluminium (25.9), even though the wood is much less dense.

questions.stem: Two points on an $E$-$\rho$ chart are aluminium alloy ($\rho=2.7$ Mg/m$^3$, $E=70$ GPa) and steel ($\rho=7.85$ Mg/m$^3$, $E=210$ GPa). Calculate the slope of the straight line joining them on the log-log chart, that is $\ln(E_2/E_1)/\ln(\rho_2/\rho_1)$ (dimensionless).
questions.explanation: $\ln(210/70)=\ln3=1.099$ and $\ln(7.85/2.7)=\ln2.907=1.067$, so the slope is $1.099/1.067=1.03$. This is almost exactly 1, which shows that steel and aluminium sit on nearly the same $E/\rho$ guideline.

questions.stem: On a modulus-density chart, the bubble for all steels is a small, tight cluster, whereas the bubble for polymers spans three or four orders of magnitude in modulus. What does this reveal?

options.text: Within steels the modulus is controlled by bond stiffness and barely changes with alloying or heat treatment, whereas in polymers it changes enormously with structure, such as cross-linking, crystallinity and temperature relative to $T_g$
Steels are all identical in composition
The chart is wrong for polymers because they are not solid
The modulus of polymers is always higher than that of steel

questions.correctOptionText: Within steels the modulus is controlled by bond stiffness and barely changes with alloying or heat treatment, whereas in polymers it changes enormously with structure, such as cross-linking, crystallinity and temperature relative to $T_g$

distractorRationale.a: Correct: bond-controlled properties vary little; structure-controlled properties vary a lot.
distractorRationale.b: Steels differ widely in composition and strength; it is the modulus that varies little.
distractorRationale.c: Polymers are solids; the large spread is real and comes from structure.
distractorRationale.d: The reverse is true: polymers have far lower moduli.

questions.explanation: Young's modulus is set mainly by the stiffness of the atomic bonds and the atomic packing, so alloying and heat treatment have little effect on it, and steels cluster at about 200 to 215 GPa. In polymers, the degree of cross-linking, crystallinity and the position of the glass transition change the modulus by orders of magnitude.

questions.stem: The bubble of a material class on an $E$-$\rho$ chart is elongated along a line of slope close to 1. What is the most reasonable interpretation?

options.text: Within the class the properties covary with density, such as in foams or woods where porosity changes both modulus and density
Density is independent of modulus within the class
Every member of the class has exactly the same modulus and the same density
The data are the result of measurement error only

questions.correctOptionText: Within the class the properties covary with density, such as in foams or woods where porosity changes both modulus and density

distractorRationale.a: Correct: a bubble stretched along a line indicates that changing density changes modulus in proportion.
distractorRationale.b: If they were independent the bubble would be roughly round.
distractorRationale.c: If that were so the class would plot as a single point, not as an extended bubble.
distractorRationale.d: The spread reflects real differences in structure within the class, not just error.

questions.explanation: A bubble stretched along a slope-1 direction shows that within the class the modulus rises or falls roughly in proportion to density, which is typical of porous materials such as foams and woods, where porosity governs both. A round bubble indicates independent variation.

questions.stem: Describe the regions occupied by metals, ceramics, polymers and composites on an $E$-$\rho$ chart and explain the difference between metals and polymers in terms of atomic bonding.
markingGuide: Metals: moduli about 10 to 400 GPa, densities about 2 to 20 Mg/m$^3$, a tight band (2 marks)
Ceramics: high moduli (to hundreds of GPa) and moderate densities (2 marks)
Polymers: low moduli (about 0.001 to 10 GPa) and low densities, about 1 Mg/m$^3$ (2 marks)
Composites: low density with high stiffness in some directions, bridging the polymer and metal regions (1 mark)
Bonding: stiffness is set by bond stiffness; metallic, ionic and covalent bonds are stiff, but polymers deform mainly by stretching weak secondary bonds and uncoiling chains (2 marks)
questions.explanation: The chart shows how bond stiffness and atomic packing set modulus and density. Metals and ceramics have strong primary bonds and so occupy the upper region, while polymers are weak between chains and so lie low.

questions.stem: A design requires a material for a light, stiff tie. A guideline of $E/\rho=40$ GPa per Mg/m$^3$ is drawn on the chart. For the candidates steel (210, 7.85), aluminium alloy (70, 2.7), titanium alloy (110, 4.5), alumina (380, 3.9), carbon-fibre composite along fibres (140, 1.55) and glass-fibre composite (40, 1.9), with values given as (E in GPa, density in Mg/m$^3$), say which lie above the line, show your working, and state two reasons why a chart ranking is not the end of the selection.
markingGuide: On the line $E=40\rho$, the required moduli at each density are 314, 108, 180, 156, 62 and 76 GPa respectively (2 marks)
Candidates above the line (modulus exceeds the line value): alumina (380>156) and carbon composite (140>62) (2 marks)
Others fall below: steel, aluminium, titanium, glass composite (2 marks)
Reason 1: alumina is brittle (poor tensile strength and toughness), so unsuitable as a tie (1 mark)
Reason 2: cost, joinability, anisotropy of the composite, or the need to check strength and other constraints (1 mark)
Shows or states that equivalent indices $E/\rho$ are 97 and 90 for the two above (1 mark)
questions.explanation: Evaluating $E/\rho$ for each (26.8, 25.9, 24.4, 97, 90 and 21) shows that only alumina and the carbon composite exceed 40. A chart screens candidates on one index; strength, toughness, cost and manufacturability must still be checked.
